findings.title: redact_value missing return-type annotation on a public, security-critical function
findings.description: redact_value(v) is a public function (no leading underscore) that sits on the security boundary — it is the function callers invoke to strip secrets before logging. It has no return-type annotation. The input type is also bare (no annotation at all). The recursive structure returns str | list | dict | <any scalar>, which is representable as a recursive TypeAlias in Python 3.10+ or as a Union in 3.9. At minimum the signature should be `def redact_value(v: object) -> object` or, better, a JsonValue TypeAlias. Without it, ty/mypy cannot verify that callers handle the return correctly, and the function is invisible to static analysis — exactly the wrong tradeoff for a security-critical path.
findings.recommendation:
Add a JsonValue recursive type alias (or use `object` for both param and return as a minimum viable fix) and annotate the function. In redact.py:

  from __future__ import annotations
  JsonValue = str | int | float | bool | None | list['JsonValue'] | dict[str, 'JsonValue']

  def redact_value(v: JsonValue) -> JsonValue: ...

findings.title: _redact_value and _redact_string also missing return-type annotations, silently diverges from redact.py interface
findings.description: log_tool_call.py inlines its own _redact_value(v) with identical logic but equally missing type annotations. Additionally, log_tool_call.py inlines the per-string pattern loop directly (no _redact_string equivalent), meaning the two copies diverge in structure. redact.py has redact_string(s: str) -> str as a named, tested, annotated step; log_tool_call.py skips that abstraction entirely and puts the loop inside the isinstance(v, str) branch. This makes it harder to unit-test the string-level redaction in log_tool_call.py in isolation.
findings.recommendation: Give _redact_value the same annotation treatment as KP-001. Extract an inline _redact_string helper to match redact.py's structure, making string-level unit testing straightforward without importing the whole module.

findings.title: Intentional duplication of _PATTERNS and _truncate_output lacks an enforcement mechanism — silent drift is the realistic failure mode
findings.description:
The module comment says 'kept in sync with hooks/lib/redact.py' and 'kept in sync with hooks/lib/jsonl-write.py'. This is a maintenance promise with no technical enforcement. The patterns cover security-sensitive paths: if a new secret type is added to redact.py's _PATTERNS and the developer forgets to mirror it to log_tool_call.py, secrets will leak into the JSONL log silently. The duplication is defensible for the stated perf reason (avoiding importlib overhead on every hook fire), but 'defensible' is not the same as 'safe without tooling'.

The truncation duplication is lower risk (correctness only, not security), but the pattern is the same: two sources of truth with no diff check.

The importlib approach is not the only alternative. A shared hooks/lib/_shared.py with an underscore-prefixed name (so it is clearly not a standalone script) would import cleanly from both redact.py and log_tool_call.py with a standard import after adding hooks/lib/__init__.py, or by manipulating sys.path. This is 3-5 lines of boilerplate, not a framework.
findings.recommendation: Either: (a) introduce hooks/lib/_core.py containing PATTERNS, redact_value, truncate_output, atomic_append and import from it in both redact.py and log_tool_call.py; or (b) add a CI/test assertion that hashes or diffs the _PATTERNS block between files and fails if they diverge. Option (a) is cleaner. Option (b) is pragmatic if option (a) is rejected on startup-latency grounds. Currently neither exists.

findings.title: Non-ENOSPC OSError from _atomic_append is silently swallowed — permission errors and path errors become invisible
findings.description: The call site for _atomic_append at line 255-258 catches OSError and returns 0 only when exc.errno == errno.ENOSPC. If the errno is anything else (EACCES, EROFS, ENOENT after makedirs fails due to a symlink loop, etc.) the except block falls through without a return, and Python falls off the end of the function returning None, which sys.exit then treats as exit code 0. This means a mis-configured log path or permission problem will silently produce no log rows ever, with no diagnostic. The intent is to never break a tool call — correct — but the right pattern is to return 0 explicitly on all OSError paths inside this module, not to let non-ENOSPC errors fall through.
findings.recommendation:
Add an explicit `return 0` after the ENOSPC check, or restructure as:

  except OSError:
      return 0

The ENOSPC-specific handling is not needed here since the behavior is the same (silent drop, exit 0). If future authors want to distinguish ENOSPC for metrics, add a comment explaining why the else path also returns 0.

findings.title: Log filename uses datetime.now() (local time) while payload timestamps use datetime.now(timezone.utc) — date-boundary mismatch
findings.description: log_file is built with `datetime.now().strftime('%Y-%m-%d')` (local time, no timezone). The `ts` field in every payload is built with `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` (UTC). For a developer in UTC-N timezones, during the hours before midnight UTC, the log file is named with today's local date but the timestamps inside it record UTC tomorrow's date. This means a log file named tool-calls-2026-04-26.jsonl can contain ts values of 2026-04-27T00:xx:xxZ. For a developer east of UTC the reverse occurs. The inconsistency will confuse log rotation and any tooling that correlates filename to record timestamps.
findings.recommendation: Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime('%Y-%m-%d')` for the log filename, matching the ts field's reference timezone. One import is already present.

findings.title: from __future__ import annotations is correct for 3.9 compat but the comment understates the scope of what it defers
findings.description: The module docstring says 'Compatible with Python 3.9+ (relies on PEP 563 deferred annotations)'. PEP 563 deferred annotations is the right mechanism for using `str | None` syntax on 3.9 (where X | Y in runtime position is a TypeError). The approach is sound. However, PEP 563 also defers all annotations, which means any code that calls typing.get_type_hints() on functions in this module at runtime (e.g. a future decorator, a test introspecting signatures) will get strings instead of types. This is a known footgun with from __future__ import annotations. Since this codebase uses ty for static analysis and does not appear to use runtime annotation inspection, the risk is low but worth acknowledging. Using Optional[str] explicitly instead would avoid the footgun entirely and make the 3.9 compatibility self-documenting without the import.
findings.recommendation: Either keep from __future__ import annotations (acceptable, lower ceremony) and note in a comment that runtime annotation inspection is unsupported, or replace the handful of X | Y annotations with Optional[X] / Union[X, Y] from typing and drop the __future__ import. The latter is more explicit for a codebase that may have other contributors unfamiliar with PEP 563 implications.

findings.title: redact_string is public but has no docstring and its public/private status is inconsistent with module usage
findings.description: redact.py is invoked as a script (not imported) in the normal flow. Its public functions redact_string and redact_value carry no leading underscore, but there is no __all__, no indication they are part of a public API, and no Google-style docstring on redact_string (redact_value has none either). The CLAUDE.md template requires Google-style docstrings on non-trivial public functions. redact_string is non-trivial in the security sense — it applies all 8 patterns sequentially. A one-line docstring explaining the ordering guarantee (patterns applied in declaration order, first match wins per position) would improve auditability of the security contract.
findings.recommendation: Add a brief Google-style docstring to redact_string noting pattern application order and any ordering guarantees, e.g.: 'Applies _PATTERNS in declaration order; all patterns are applied to every string (not first-match-stop).' This also makes the behavior difference from a hypothetical future regex alternation explicit.

residual_risks.description: Pattern divergence between redact.py and log_tool_call.py is the primary residual risk. If a developer adds a new secret type to redact.py (as the docs suggest is the intended workflow) and does not manually mirror it to log_tool_call.py, secrets will enter the JSONL log. The test suite tests redact.py directly but does not appear to test log_tool_call.py's _redact_value independently. This risk is present today and grows linearly with each new pattern added.

The fallback pairing logic in the post-event handler (lines 210-228) reads the most-recent temp file matching the session prefix when the hash-matched file is not found. Under concurrent tool calls within the same session, this fallback can pair the wrong pre-event's timestamp with a post-event, producing a plausible-looking but incorrect duration_ms. This is a silent data quality issue, not a correctness or security bug, but worth noting for anyone relying on duration_ms for performance analysis.

_atomic_append uses os.makedirs on dirname(path). If path is a bare filename (no directory component), dirname returns '' and the `or '.'` fallback calls os.makedirs('.', exist_ok=True), which is harmless but unexpected. The real risk is that log_file is constructed with Path.home() so dirname will always be non-empty in normal operation. However if Path.home() raises (rare but possible in container environments with no HOME), the exception is not caught inside main() at that point and would propagate to the outer except Exception guard in __main__, silently swallowing it. The log_dir and log_file construction should be inside the try block.

testing_gaps.description: No test directly invokes log_tool_call.py's internal _redact_value and compares it against redact.py's redact_value for the same inputs. The existing test-redaction.sh tests redact.py via subprocess but does not run the same payloads through log_tool_call.py. This means the two implementations could diverge and the test suite would not catch it.

The UTC vs local-time log filename bug (KP-005) has no test. A test that sets TZ=America/New_York and runs a post-event near midnight UTC would reproduce the mismatch. Currently no timezone-aware test exists for the log file naming path.

The non-ENOSPC OSError fall-through in _atomic_append (KP-004) is untested. A test that passes a read-only log path (or mocks os.open to raise EACCES) would confirm exit code 0 is returned and not None/non-zero.
